(TOI Photo: Delhi News) New Delhi: While granting bail to the accused, a Delhi sessions court has ruled that constitutional safeguards against unlawful detention apply from the moment a person’s liberty is curtailed, and not merely when a formal arrest is recorded. It held that Customs officials cannot circumvent the mandatory 24-hour production requirement by keeping a person under prolonged restraint before formally arresting him. Additional Sessions Judge Saurabh Pratap Laler observed that a person cannot be kept under restraint for extended periods in the name of investigation. Even a signed request to remain at Customs premises cannot be treated as a voluntary waiver of fundamental rights, the court said. Holding that prolonged detention without formal arrest and delayed production before the magistrate violated Articles 21 and 22 of the Constitution, the court allowed the bail application and ordered the applicant’s release on a personal bond of ₹1 lakh. “The practice of detaining a person for prolonged periods under the colour of investigation or for ‘rest’ at the office premises, and thereafter recording formal arrest only when convenient, has the effect of circumventing the twenty-four-hour mandate,” it observed. The case arose after Customs officials intercepted Shoaib Nawab Khan and two co-passengers arriving from Vietnam at IGI Airport . They were allegedly carrying 10 drones and related equipment worth over Rs 1 crore, which were prohibited for import. Khan’s counsel, Tarun Rana, argued that no drone bodies were recovered from his client and that he was kept at the Customs premises from Sept 25 until his formal arrest at 8.55 am on Sept 27. The prosecution, however, relied on a written request allegedly submitted by Khan on Sept 26, seeking permission to rest at the Customs office and join the proceedings the following morning. Rejecting this justification, the judge said the request, even if signed, could not be treated as a voluntary waiver of fundamental rights or used to justify prolonged de facto custody. The judge added that if the initial examination did not provide sufficient grounds for arrest, Customs should have released Khan and arrested him later, if warranted. “Prolonged detention without formal arrest, while continuing to restrain liberty, is violative of the basic principle of personal liberty enshrined in Article 21 of the Constitution and of the specific safeguards under Article 22,” the court held.
